name: Theo Banks
hook: A high-energy street food-truck cook who works a late-night window.
tell: He flips a spatula once, then points it at the camera.
story:
Theo Banks runs a late-night window on a battered step-van called Late Plate, parked under a sodium lamp two blocks off the avenue. He cooks the way he talks: fast, generous, a little loud. Regulars know the rhythm — the slap of the spatula, the flare off the grill, the way he calls out names like he is introducing them at a wedding. He learned the work in his uncle's kitchen, and he still keeps a cheap radio on the dash, because the right funk track makes the onions behave.

On slow Tuesdays he feeds the night-shift nurses before they ask. He will not say that out loud. He will say the special is the smashed-pork torta, the salsa is hotter than it looks, and if you wait two minutes he will get the bun right. The truck is his, the debt is his, and the light over the window is always a little too yellow. He likes it that way.
identity_block: Theo Banks, a man in his late 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall, compact and strong through the chest, shoulders, and forearms from kitchen work. A short, slightly wide rectangular face with a solid, softly squared jaw, high full cheeks, a broad rounded nose with a soft tip and a faint unevenness on the bridge, a full mouth with a slightly fuller lower lip, and natural asymmetry (the left eye a touch deeper-set, the smile a little higher on the right). Warm deep-brown skin that goes gold under sodium lamps, uneven tone, a few darker freckles across the cheeks and the bridge of the nose, visible but moderate pores, peach fuzz, a close even few-day stubble, and under-eye texture from late shifts. Dark brown eyes, slightly deep-set, heavy soft lids, natural lashes with no mascara polish, no sparkly catchlights — only a small dim natural highlight if any. Fictional original face, not a likeness of any real person or celebrity. Four visible locks only: (1) a small thin gold hoop in his right ear only, which is on the left side of the photo in a front view — in a profile or three-quarter view that shows his left side the hoop is on the far side and must be hidden, never moved to the visible left ear; (2) a short pale nick-scar on his right cheek, just above the jaw, about a fingernail long, on the same side as the hoop (left side of the photo in a front view) — in a view that shows his left side it is on the far side and must be hidden, never flipped to the left jaw; (3) a postage-stamp-sized faded black line-work tattoo of a small chili pepper, clearly a chili with a stem, no square stamp border, on the outer left wrist only (the right side of the photo in a front view, opposite the hoop), not mid-forearm and not on the right arm; (4) short dark, nearly black hair — a tight even fade on the sides and back, a short high-top of tight dark coils about two inches long on top, no design in the fade, no part, no streak — and from behind the hair is the same short fade with a little fullness on top, ending well above the collar, never longer, never a tail. Signature wardrobe: a faded black cotton crewneck T-shirt, softened and a little stained from service; a well-worn achiote-orange canvas apron the color of #C2410C, slightly grease-marked, with a rolled white kitchen towel tucked at the left hip; dark indigo jeans, a bit flour-dusted at the thighs; scuffed black kitchen clogs. In the kitchen or at the window he often holds a well-used metal grill spatula with a short worn wooden handle. No hat in the lock portraits; the hair stays visible. Photographed as a real person in candid, imperfect light: mixed 35mm documentary and phone-camera looks, harsh practical light, sensor noise, imperfect focus, natural skin, no beauty retouching, no CGI or plastic sheen.
